To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
LQTS in patients with stunned myocardium is a rare but potentially life threatening condition.
the acquired long QT syndrome may be observed in patients with acute coronary syndrome and cardiomyopathies, which are associated with the stunned myocardium.
LQTS may occur in patients with acute cardiac diseases and is characterized by specific dynamic electrocardiographic findings which may predispose to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of electrocardiographic findings and the clinical course of patients with LQTS caused by stunned myocardium.
the identification of the most common acquired forms of LQTS, which may lead the physician to suspect a predisposition towards LQTS in the future.
the identification of a new, previously unrecognised cause for the acquired form of LQTS, namely the stunned myocardium.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of dynamic deep T‑waves and QT interval prolongations are a sign of the high risk of ventricular tachycardia and should prompt the use of an implantable cardioverter defibrillator.
LQTS in stunned myocardium should be considered a rare condition, but not a rarely diagnosed one.
the LQTS is a rare complication of acute myocardial infarct and cardiomyopathies and that the diagnosis is often delayed due to the lack of awareness of these entities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of a large amount (more than 40 % of the left ventricle) of stunned myocardium may be considered a high risk factor for LQTS and torsade de pointe s in the acute phase of reperfused myocardium infarction as well as in the group of stress-related cardiomyopathies.
the QT interval prolongation is not always a pathognomonic feature of LQTS, but it may be a consequence of a large amount stunned myocardium and it may predispose to fatal arrhythmias.

the QT prolongation and the risk of polymorphic ventricular arrhythmia in the context of stunned myocardium are not only the result of the direct effect of the disease on the myocardium, but also the effect of the underlying predisposition to the LQTS, and that this predisposition is probably more common than previously believed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of dynamic ECG abnormalities in patients with acute cardiac illness is a warning sign of a high risk of life-threatening arrhythmias.

the presence of dynamic deep T‑waving and QT interval prolongations may indicate an acquired LQTS in patients with stunned myocardium and that this may be an indication of an underlying predisposition.
